item.title: Rick Moranis, Cameron Diaz and Lindsay Lohan among stars who left fame behind before returning to Hollywood
item.description: From Rick Moranis to Cameron Diaz and Lindsay Lohan, these Hollywood stars walked away from fame and made remarkable comebacks years later on screen.
item.content:encoded:
Rick Moranis is stepping back into the spotlight after decades away from Hollywood, joining a growing list of stars who left fame behind and later returned.

The 71-year-old actor is taking on his first live-action part in nearly 30 years after walking away from the entertainment industry at the height of his career following a family tragedy.

Now, Moranis is reprising his role as Lord Dark Helmet in "Spaceballs: The New One," the long-awaited sequel to Mel Brooks' 1987 cult classic science-fiction comedy movie "Spaceballs."

'DEADPOOL' STAR ROB DELANEY REVEALS HOW LOSING 2-YEAR-OLD SON CHANGED HIS APPROACH TO FAME

In July, Moranis made a rare public appearance to promote the sequel at San Diego Comic-Con, where he received a standing ovation when he appeared on stage wearing his character's signature massive black helmet. Moranis participated in a panel discussion alongside co-stars Daphne Zuniga, Josh Gad, Keke Palmer and Lewis Pullman as well as director Josh Greenbaum and screenwriters Benji Samit and Dan Hernandez.

Zuniga is reprising her role as Princess Vespa while other original stars who returned for the sequel include George Wyner as Colonel Sandurz, Bill Pullman as Lone Starr and Brooks as Yogurt.

During the panel, Moranis revealed what finally brought him back in front of the camera after his decades-long hiatus.

"This came along right at the right time, and I started talking to these folks and hearing who was going to be in it," Moranis said, via People. "I spoke to Josh Greenbaum and I heard that Bill Pullman was coming back and that Lewis was going to be in it too, and it just felt like this is it. It’s time and — yes. I said yes, and it is the best decision I’ve ever made."

Moranis became one of Hollywood's most recognizable comedy stars in the 1980s and 1990s after starring in a string of hit movies including "Spaceballs," "Ghostbusters," "Little Shop of Horrors," "Honey, I Shrunk the Kids," "Parenthood," "My Blue Heaven" and "The Flintstones."

However, after his wife, costume designer Ann Belsky, died in 1991 following a battle with breast cancer, Moranis stepped away from show business to focus on raising their two children, daughter Rachel and son Mitchell. He last appeared on-screen in 1997's "Honey, We Shrunk Ourselves," the third installment in the "Honey, I Shrunk the Kids" movie series.

During a 2015 interview with the Hollywood Reporter, Moranis reflected on his decision to prioritize his family over his career.

"I was working with really interesting people, wonderful people," he said. "I went from that to being at home with a couple of little kids, which is a very different lifestyle. But it was important to me. I have absolutely no regrets whatsoever. My life is wonderful."

Moranis also clarified that he had not officially retired from acting, telling the outlet, "I took a break, which turned into a longer break."

"But I’m interested in anything that I would find interesting," he continued. "I still get the occasional query about a film or television role and as soon as one comes along that piques my interest, I'll probably do it."

MATT DAMON SAYS HOLLYWOOD'S 'RUTHLESS' NATURE HAS TAKEN HIM AWAY FROM FATHERHOOD MORE THAN HE'D LIKE

"I’m happy with the things I said yes to, and I’m very happy with the many things I’ve said no to," Moranis added. "Yes, I am picky, and I’ll continue to be picky. Picky has worked for me."

Though Moranis left live-action films behind for many years, he continued working occasionally as a voice actor. He first dipped his toe back into the movie business in 2001, voicing two characters in "Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer & the Island of Misfit Toys." Some of his other voice-acting gigs include "Brother Bear," "The Animated Adventures of Bob & Doug McKenzie," and the voice of Dark Helmet in "The Goldbergs."

During his appearance at Comic-Con, Moranis once again set the record straight regarding the perception that he had retired as he revealed that he and Brooks had long discussed making a follow-up to "Spaceballs."

"Actually, I started talking to Mel about the sequel in 1989," he said. "We kept talking about it."

"I really wasn’t retired; I was just negotiating," Moranis joked.

STOCKARD CHANNING HITS FIRST RED CARPET IN 2 YEARS AFTER SAYING SHE'S A 'RECLUSE'

While Moranis’ return has drawn renewed attention due to his decades-long absence, other stars have also taken long breaks from Hollywood before making high-profile comebacks. Here's a look at several celebrities who stepped away from the spotlight for years before finding their way back to the screen.

Cameron Diaz was one of Hollywood’s most bankable stars when she quietly stepped away from acting in 2014.

Diaz made her breakthrough in 1994's "The Mask" and went on to star in a series of hit films including "There’s Something About Mary," "My Best Friend's Wedding," "Charlie's Angels," "My Sister's Keeper," "Shrek" and "The Other Woman," among others.

After starring in 2014's "Annie," Diaz walked away from show business to focus on building a life with husband Benji Madden.

"It felt like the right thing for me to reclaim my own life, and I just really didn't care about anything else," the actress said during a 2025 appearance at Fortune's Most Powerful Women Summit, according to E! News.

"Nobody's opinion, nobody's success, no one's offer, no one's anything could change my mind about my decision of taking care of myself and building the life that I really wanted to have. I think it really comes to what are you passionate about? For me, it was to build my family."

During her break, Diaz welcomed daughter Raddix, 6, and son Cardinal, 2, with Madden and launched her Avaline wine brand. The couple's third child, son Nautus, was born in May.

After a decade away from movies, Diaz returned to the screen in Netflix’s 2025 action comedy "Back in Action," starring opposite Jamie Foxx. She has since lined up other projects including Netflix’s "Bad Day," Apple TV+’s "Outcome" and "Shrek 5," in which she will reprise her voice role as Princess Fiona.

Lindsay Lohan’s comeback followed years of intense public scrutiny and a long stretch away from major studio films.

Lohan became one of Hollywood’s biggest young stars after breaking out in "The Parent Trap" and later leading hits including "Freaky Friday," "Mean Girls" and "Herbie: Fully Loaded."

However, Lohan's promising career was derailed by multiple box-office flops and a string of highly-publicized legal problems and substance abuse issues. After years of tabloid attention and personal struggles, Lohan left the United States in 2014 and eventually relocated full-time to Dubai, spending much of the next decade outside the Hollywood spotlight. She told Emirates Woman in 2018 that moving to Dubai afforded her "a fresh start."

Lohan began rebuilding her acting career with Netflix’s 2022 holiday movie "Falling for Christmas," followed by more streaming projects and a major return to one of her signature roles in "Freakier Friday."

During a 2025 interview with The Sunday Times, Lohan said she stepped away because she had lost her excitement for making movies and wanted "a more private life, a real life," before returning once she felt "that itch again."

Lohan will next be seen in Hulu’s "Count My Lies," a limited series in which she stars opposite Shailene Woodley and Kit Harington.

Ke Huy Quan’s Hollywood disappearance ended with one of the industry’s most celebrated comeback stories.

Quan became a child star after playing Short Round opposite Harrison Ford in 1984’s "Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom" and Data in 1985’s "The Goonies." However, Ke only landed a few minor TV and film roles after his early fame and found himself being offered stereotypical parts geared toward Asians.

During a 2023 interview with People, Quan said that he made the "very difficult decision" to walk away from acting in the early 2000s. He then spent years working behind the camera as a stunt coordinator and assistant director.

However, he recalled that after seeing 2018’s "Crazy Rich Asians", he was inspired to revisit his first love.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I was happy working behind the camera, but I had serious FOMO (fear of missing out)," Ke told the outlet. "I wanted to be up there with my fellow Asian actors."

After roughly two decades away from acting, Quan returned in 2022’s "Everything Everywhere All at Once," a role that earned him the Academy Award for best supporting actor. In his emotional Oscars speech, Quan reflected on his unlikely journey, saying, "Dreams are something you have to believe in. I almost gave up on mine."

Daniel Day-Lewis has stepped away from Hollywood more than once, but his latest return marked the end of what many believed was a permanent retirement.

Known for his intensely selective approach to roles, Day-Lewis has previously taken long breaks throughout his career. After starring in 1997’s "The Boxer," Day-Lewis retreated from acting and spent several years in Italy learning shoemaking before returning in Martin Scorsese’s 2002 film "Gangs of New York."

The three-time Oscar winner announced he was retiring from acting after starring in 2017’s "Phantom Thread." At the time, his representative said, "Daniel Day-Lewis will no longer be working as an actor. He is immensely grateful to all of his collaborators and audiences over the many years. This is a private decision and neither he nor his representatives will make any further comment on this subject."

Eight years later, his son, Ronan Day-Lewis, persuaded him to co-write and star in the 2025 drama "Anemone."

Day-Lewis later pushed back on the idea that he ever meant to permanently retire.

In a 2025 Rolling Stone interview, Day-Lewis said he "never intended to retire, really," and called his earlier retirement announcement "grandiose gibberish." He explained that he still loved the work, but struggled with the lifestyle around filmmaking and felt "hollowed out" after "Phantom Thread."

He said returning for "Anemone" was largely about working with Ronan, who directed the film. Day-Lewis said that collaboration brought the spark back, saying, "working with Ro, that furnace just lit up."

Renée Zellweger stepped away from Hollywood after years of working at a relentless pace.

Zellweger became one of the most prominent actresses of the late 1990s and 2000s with roles in the hit movies "Jerry Maguire," "Bridget Jones’s Diary," "Chicago," "Cold Mountain" and "Cinderella Man." But after 2010’s "My Own Love Song," Zellweger took a six-year break from acting.

During a 2025 interview with British Vogue, Zellweger explained why she decided to pause her career.

"I was sick of the sound of my own voice. When I was working, I was like, ‘Oh my gosh, listen to you. Are you sad again, Renée? Oh, is this your mad voice?’ It was a regurgitation of the same emotional experiences," she said.

Zellweger told the outlet that her hiatus from acting enabled her to pursue other projects and embrace a healthier lifestyle.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"I wrote music and studied international law," she said. "I built a house, rescued a pair of older doggies, created a partnership that led to a production company, advocated for and fundraised with a sick friend, and spent a lot of time with family and godchildren and driving across the country with the dogs. I got healthy."

Zellweger returned in 2016 with the hit sequel "Bridget Jones’s Baby." She went on to earn some of the strongest reviews of her career for playing Judy Garland in 2019’s "Judy" and her performance earned her the Academy Award for best actress. Zellweger previously won the best supporting actress Oscar for her performance in "Cold Mountain."

Macaulay Culkin walked away from Hollywood after becoming one of the most famous child stars in the world.

Culkin shot to superstardom as Kevin McCallister in 1990’s "Home Alone" and its 1992 sequel, "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York." He went on to star in hit films including "My Girl," "The Good Son" and "Richie Rich."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

After filming "Richie Rich," Culkin stepped away from acting, later explaining that he wanted to attend school, date and spend time with people his own age.

He returned nine years later with "Party Monster" and has continued accepting occasional projects on his own terms, including roles in "Saved!," "American Horror Story: Double Feature" and "The Righteous Gemstones."

Pamela Anderson’s return to the spotlight has become one of Hollywood’s more unexpected late-career reinventions.

Anderson became a global sex symbol in the 1990s through "Baywatch," Playboy and years of tabloid attention that often overshadowed her acting ambitions. After decades of being defined by her image and personal life, she retreated to Vancouver Island, embraced a quieter lifestyle and began reassessing the public persona that had followed her for much of her career.

Her comeback began with a wave of projects that allowed her to reclaim her own story, including the 2023 Netflix documentary "Pamela, a Love Story" and her memoir, "Love, Pamela." She made her Broadway debut in "Chicago" in 2022 and earned some of the strongest reviews of her career for "The Last Showgirl," along with Golden Globe and SAG nominations.

item.title: Trump weighs in on Lindsay Clancy murder trial dubbed 'kangaroo court' by GOP leaders
item.description: Trump says Lindsay Clancy will pay "the price" after a mistrial was declared when the jury deadlocked 11-1 in the Massachusetts murder case.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump said Lindsay Clancy will still have to pay "the price" for the deaths of her three small children — Cora 5, Dawson 3, and Callan, 8 months — after a mistrial was ruled on Friday.

During a press gaggle in the Oval Office, a reporter asked Trump if he'd been following the murder trial of Clancy, a Massachusetts mom whose defense did not deny that she strangled her children with exercise bands in January 2023, but argued that she was not guilty by reason of insanity. Her attorneys claimed that she suffered from postpartum psychosis, a severe but rare psychiatric condition in which a person is disconnected from reality.

"It's a horrible tragedy," Trump shared with reporters. "It's a horrible tragedy. I see what's happened, and it looks like it's a hung jury."

"I assume there's going to be another trial. It's a terrible situation. Look, she did a horrible, horrible thing. Can't be worse. But you'll find out what the price to pay is. There'll be a price. It's going to be [a] mental institution or jail or something," Trump continued.

LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL DECLARED AFTER JURY DEADLOCKS IN KILLINGS OF HER THREE CHILDREN

The six-week trial, which was supposed to determine whether Clancy was to be held criminally responsible, quickly evolved into a flashpoint in the internet culture war over women's postpartum mental health and spurred misinformation and conspiracy theories, including false claims accusing her ex-husband, Patrick Clancy, of being responsible for the children’s deaths.

After nearly a week of deliberations, Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial when the jury deadlocked 11 to 1: 11 jurors voted to acquit Clancy, while one holdout refused to join them. The jury consisted of 9 women and 3 men.

PROSECUTOR IN INFAMOUS KILLER MOM CASE SAYS WOMEN ON LINDSAY CLANCY JURY MAY BRING ‘STRANGE TWIST’ TO VERDICT

Clancy's defense attorney requested that the lone juror be removed because a note given to the judge by the jurors said the holdout had doubt but refused to apply it, according to People.

The mistrial invoked a strong reaction from Republican lawmakers, while Democratic lawmakers and leaders — including those from Clancy's state — have remained mum on the high-profile case.

"Out of 12 people, only ONE had the courage to hold a serial killer accountable for her actions," Rep. Michael Rulli, R-Ohio, posted on X. "That’s not just bravery. That’s a hero."

"Holdout juror’s going to need security," Sen. Mike Lee, R-Ohio, posted on X. "Sad."

Florida Republican Governor Ron DeSantis called the mistrial a "miscarriage of justice."

"The victims deserved far, far better than a kangaroo court," DeSantis wrote.

Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., who has been incredibly vocal against Clancy's supporters — who have been gathered outside the courthouse and posted videos showing support online — suggesting Clancy would not have this support if she were Black.

"This case is not about the excuses for why she committed murder," Mace posted on X. "This is about justice for the three beautiful souls whose lives were taken after their mother strangled them with her bare hands and workout bands."

PATRICK CLANCY SPEAKS OUT AFTER HUNG JURY IN LINDSAY CLANCY CASE, ADDRESSES PROSPECT OF ANOTHER TRIAL

"12 jurors looked at this onesie," Mace continued. "Only ONE stood his ground to defend the children."

But Clancy's defense argued that she was a devoted and loving mother who was desperately seeking to get help, alleging that the cocktail of medications she was on worsened her mental state. Clancy had been prescribed 13 psychiatric medications — more than 30 prescriptions — in the four months leading up to the murders.

Patrick Clancy is suing for wrongful death and medical malpractice against Clancy's providers, Dr. Jennifer Tufts, Rebecca Jollotta, Aster Mental Health and South Shore Health System. Clancy also filed a separate lawsuit alleging negligence, medical malpractice and personal injury.

"Lindsay was struggling. We were all very concerned," Susan Clancy, Clancy's mother-in-law, told jurors. "She was very nurturing, very loving. She was a wonderful mother. Wonderful."

Clancy is due back in court Sept. 29 for a status hearing, trial assignment and a defense Rule 25 motion.

item.title: AI robot pet could know your family too well
item.description: The OlloNi SS1 AI robot pet uses a 4K camera and facial recognition to learn your family, but its removable Red Heart memory module raises questions.
item.content:encoded:
We've covered home robots that can fold laundry and others designed to become AI companions. Now there's one that wants to remember your family. The OlloNi SS1 is an AI robot pet that can recognize family members and pets as it moves around your home. OlloBot says it can learn your routines, respond to emotional cues and save memorable family moments along the way.

Here's where it gets really interesting. OlloNi has a removable "Red Heart" memory module designed to carry those memories into a future OlloBot. So, when the robot gets replaced, years of personalization could move right along with you.

I can see the appeal of that. I also think it's important to ask yourself this: How much of your family's life are you comfortable letting a robot remember? Here's how OlloNi works, what it can remember and the privacy questions to consider before deciding whether you'd want one in your home.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.

WOULD YOU PAY $8,000 FOR A ROBOT TO FOLD LAUNDRY?

The OlloNi SS1 is OlloBot's newest AI companion robot pet, developed by Hong Kong-based Ollobot Robotics Limited. Unlike a robot built mainly for chores, the SS1 is designed to interact with the people and pets living around it.

Two circular eye screens display expressions while a separate main screen handles information and direct interaction. The setup gives OlloNi a face that can react visually without relying on spoken responses every time.

A 4K camera with motion tracking helps the robot recognize individual family members and household pets. OlloBot says the SS1 gradually learns routines and preferences as it spends more time with a household. It also adapts to different communication patterns.

That puts OlloNi in a different category from a robot vacuum or a machine built mainly to handle physical work. The goal here is to make the robot feel increasingly familiar.

OlloBot is also giving the SS1 what it describes as proactive emotional interaction. The company says the robot uses several types of information to interpret what is happening around it. That includes someone's tone of voice and facial expression. It can also learn behavioral patterns over time.

For example, OlloBot says the robot may notice when someone appears to be feeling low. Instead of waiting for that person to issue a command, OlloNi could approach and initiate an interaction.

We recently covered Familiar, another emotionally aware AI robot pet. That robot is also designed to learn routines and react to the people around it. OlloNi takes the idea in another direction by connecting that personalization to a memory system that can survive beyond the original robot.

One feature I can see families using is OlloNi's 4K camera. With permission turned on, OlloBot says the SS1 can recognize moments such as laughter or celebrations and capture them automatically. Its AI-assisted Vlog feature can then edit the footage and add music to create home videos.

I like the idea behind this. When something memorable happens, someone usually reaches for a phone. That often means the person recording ends up watching part of the moment through a screen.

OlloNi could change that. Because the robot is already moving around the home, it could capture moments while everyone else stays in them.

But this is also where I would start thinking seriously about privacy. You are allowing a connected 4K camera to move around your home and decide which moments may be worth saving.

That is a lot of access to give any device, no matter how cute the robot looks.

OlloNi also supports remote viewing and two-way voice and video calls. Unlike a camera sitting on a shelf, the robot can move around the home and follow activity. OlloBot says this could make remote check-ins feel more active for family members who live apart.

The idea could appeal to someone who wants to stay connected with an older relative or other family members from a distance. OlloBot's website also says its app can let you see and interact with OlloNi while you are away. The app is designed to show daily moments and memories the robot has captured.

However, remote access raises the stakes for security. A camera that can move around your house deserves strong account protection. Owners should know exactly who can connect to it and what happens if an account gets compromised.

This may be the most unusual part of the SS1. OlloBot calls it the Red Heart. The detachable module has 16GB of RAM and 64GB of local storage. OlloBot says the module carries the robot's long-term memories and personalized information.

Now imagine replacing the robot several years from now. Instead of starting over, OlloBot says you could move the Red Heart into a future-generation OlloBot. Family memories and personalized information could then follow you to the next device. That is a clever idea. Most gadgets become disposable once their hardware gets old. OlloBot wants the relationship you developed with this one to survive the upgrade.

At the same time, think about how personal that little module could become. Years of family life could potentially be tied to it. That makes the Red Heart something I would want protected every bit as carefully as the robot itself.

This is where I would slow down and read the fine print. OlloBot says the SS1 uses local encrypted processing and includes a physical camera cover. The company also says facial recognition and automatic family-moment capture work with your permission.

Those are good things to see. Still, a robot that can move around your home, recognize faces and build memories over time deserves more than a quick glance at the privacy settings. OlloBot's current privacy policy was last updated July 6, 2026. It covers the company's store and broader Services, including device and usage information collected when people interact with those Services. The policy also says some information may be handled by outside vendors that provide services such as IT management, data analytics or cloud storage.

What I want to see next is something much more specific to the SS1 itself. If this robot can recognize your family and save moments inside your home, you should know exactly where that information goes. OlloBot should explain what stays on the Red Heart, what leaves the robot and how long anything gets stored.

I would also want a clear answer about deletion. If OlloNi spends years learning your routines and how your family interacts, you should be able to see what it knows and permanently erase that information when you want it gone.

AI WEARABLE WATCHES YOU TO PREDICT WHAT YOU NEED

There is another privacy point worth watching. OlloBot's Aug. 28 announcement lists children separated from their parents by distance among the potential users for the SS1.

Meanwhile, OlloBot's current privacy policy says its "Services are not intended to be used by children". It also says the company does not knowingly collect personal information from children under the age of majority in the user's jurisdiction. That does not automatically mean there is a conflict.

The current policy appears geared largely toward OlloBot's store and broader services rather than offering a detailed privacy framework specifically for the SS1. Still, OlloBot should clarify how those terms apply when a product is designed to interact with families and potentially children inside the home. Parents should not have to guess.

This is one of the first questions I would ask about the Red Heart: What happens if you lose it? If your family has used OlloNi for years, that little removable module could contain a very personal history of life inside your home.

OlloBot says the SS1 uses local encrypted processing, which is encouraging. What I want to know is what happens when the Red Heart comes out of the robot. If someone finds or steals it, does the information remain encrypted and inaccessible? I would also want a way to remotely erase the module if it disappears.

The whole appeal of the Red Heart is that families could keep it for years and move their memories into a future OlloBot. If OlloBot wants us to hold onto something that personal for that long, I want to know exactly how it will keep those memories protected.

OlloNi goes beyond watching the people around it. The robot also pays attention to what is happening inside the home. OlloBot says the SS1 includes temperature and humidity sensors along with ambient light and spatial sensors. That gives the robot more context about its surroundings. The company says those sensors can help with reminders and brief activity records tied to relevant interactions rather than continuous recording.

If all of this has you wondering what the robot costs, there is a catch. You cannot back the planned SS1 crowdfunding campaign right now.

OlloBot previously said it would launch the OlloNi SS1 globally on Kickstarter in August 2026. In July, the company narrowed that window to late August. Then the plan changed.

On Aug. 28, OlloBot announced that it had postponed the crowdfunding launch. The company pointed to recent changes in the U.S. regulatory and market-access environment for robotic devices made abroad. OlloBot says it wants a clear path to market and fulfillment before moving forward.

For now, the company has not announced a new crowdfunding date. OlloBot says it will share an updated timeline through its official channels once one is confirmed. So, consider the SS1 a robot to watch rather than one you can order today.

OlloNi SS1 shows how quickly the idea of a home robot is changing. We have spent years watching robots get better at physical work. Now companies want these machines to learn about the people living around them. That changes what you need to consider before bringing one home.

With a robot like OlloNi, start by looking beyond the cute eyes. Find out what its camera records and who can access those recordings. Next, understand the memory system.

You should know what stays locally on the robot and what gets transmitted elsewhere. Also check whether you can permanently delete information when you want it gone. Remote access deserves attention too. Look for strong account security and controls that let you shut off features you do not use.

Finally, think about the lifespan of your data. The entire point of the Red Heart is to keep personalized information after you replace the robot. That makes long-term software support especially important.

We recently saw why connected robots deserve scrutiny when a security report raised concerns about a Yarbo robot mower. The issues involved remote access, cameras and home-network exposure. Yarbo later acknowledged the core technical findings and began rolling out fixes.

OlloBot has already said it uses local encrypted processing and includes a physical camera cover. Now I want to see the deeper security details behind those promises. We reached out to OlloBot with questions about data storage, remote access and Red Heart security but did not hear back before our deadline.

MAJORITY OF YOUNG ADULTS SAY THEY ARE 'MORE CONCERNED THAN EXCITED' ABOUT AI: PEW RESEARCH

OlloNi SS1 caught my attention because OlloBot wants this robot to become more personal the longer it lives with you. The Red Heart is the feature I keep coming back to. Instead of losing years of personalization when the hardware gets old, your family's memories could move into the next robot. I can see why that might feel special. I can also see why some people will want the exact opposite. A robot that recognizes your family and captures private moments can learn a lot about what happens behind your front door. When those memories are designed to last for years, privacy becomes part of the buying decision from day one. OlloBot's physical camera cover and local encrypted processing are good places to start. Before anyone hands over money, though, I want clearer answers about recordings and remote access. The company also needs to explain exactly what happens to information stored in the Red Heart. That does not make OlloNi a robot to fear. It makes it a robot that asks for a lot of trust.

Would you want an AI pet remembering years of your family's life and carrying those memories into its next robot body, or would that feel like giving a machine too much access to your home? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

item.title: Michigan State offensive lineman unleashes a fountain of puke during two-point conversion
item.description: Michigan State's Robert Wright Jr. unleashed a vomit-filled two-point conversion block in Pat Fitzgerald's debut win over Toledo Friday night.
item.content:encoded:
This weekend features the first "full" slate of college football, but eagle-eyed fans were able to find some pretty premier programs take the field before Saturday.

Perennial top-25 programs like Missouri, and Utah were in action on Thursday and we were even treated to some college football themed Friday Night Lights.

The vaunted Miami Hurricanes were able to obliterate an undermanned Stanford team out west, and the Michigan State Spartans kicked off the Pat Fitzgerald era in style with a 30-20 win over MAC darlings Toledo on Friday.

SEC LAWYERS, LANE KIFFIN AND DEATH VALLEY: COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S WEEK 1 IS SET FOR FIREWORKS

And it is in East Lansing where we find our story today.

As Sparty was trailing by a single point early in the fourth quarter, quarterback Alessio Milivojevic connected with Rodney Bullard Jr. for a five-yard touchdown to put Michigan State ahead for good.

To put themselves ahead by a whole touchdown and extra point, Fitzgerald and the staff decided to go for two, and that's when offensive coordinator Nick Sheridan reached into his bag of tricks and pulled out the sickest two-point conversion play he had.

Literally.

That's a lot of puke, brother.

This could be karmic payback for making everyone watch Michigan State play in those highlighter green uniforms from a few years ago.

Those were enough to make anyone in attendance need to grab a bucket.

WEEK ONE UPSET SPECIAL: THESE THREE COLLEGE FOOTBALL TEAMS SHOULD BE ON UPSET ALERT THIS WEEKEND

Let this be a note to offensive linemen everywhere who are plying their craft, if you're having trouble picking up twists and stunts along the defensive line, just unleash your pregame meal right as the ball is snapped.

No one is going to want to touch you and your chunder without throwing on a hazmat suit first.

It's brilliant, really.

Oh, and the two-point conversion was good, proving even further that this was a calculated move by the Spartans and right tackle Robert Wright Jr.

It's a fairly untapped technique, considering most linemen I see puking do it in the huddle or right before the ball is snapped.

Wright, on the other hand, waited until after the ball was snapped, picks up a stunting interior lineman, passes off the rush end, and keeps his quarterback clean for a successful two-point try.

That's consummate professionalism right there!

Now all he needs is an NIL deal with Pepto-Bismol and he's in business; make it happen, Sparty!

item.title: Students divided as University of Michigan will hide first-semester grades for 2027 freshmen
item.description: University of Michigan students clash over a pass/fail policy hiding first-semester freshman grades, debating mental health relief vs. study habits.
item.content:encoded:
ANN ARBOR, Mich. — University of Michigan students are split over a new administrative policy that will hide first-semester letter grades for incoming freshmen, with some welcoming the relief from academic pressure while others warn it could coddle students and fail to prepare them for the real world.

Starting in fall 2027, incoming first-year students enrolled in the university’s College of Literature, Science, and the Arts (LSA) will have their first-semester transcript grades designated strictly as pass (P) or no credit (NC). School officials say the pilot program aims to combat a growing "mental health crisis" on college campuses and ease the transition from high school to college. 

"Our goal is to help first-year students acclimate to the demands of college and allow intrinsic motivations to guide personally meaningful academic journeys — core elements of a liberal arts and sciences education," the university stated in its announcement.

COLLEGE STUDENTS EXPRESS STRONG TRUST IN SCHOOL LEADERS DESPITE BROADER PUBLIC CYNICISM: GALLUP

While students will still receive traditional letter grades and feedback directly from professors throughout the term, final marks will not appear on official external transcripts or factor into overall GPAs. The university will retain internal letter grade records for advising, financial aid eligibility, academic awards and scholarships, and other administrative purposes.

Several students told Fox News Digital that easing into college expectations could be a net positive.

"If there are measures to ease the way for high school students coming to [university], I think that's a good thing," said Alexander, an exchange grad student from Austria.

Ella Langlois, an LSA student, said that it does not hurt to give the policy a test run. 

"I do think mental health is always super important," she said.

William Bushey, a civil engineering major, called the decision a "good call."

"I'm an engineer, so I go through all the weeder classes all the time," Bushey said. "There's a lot of successful people who struggle in their first-year classes, but will just pass and then wind up being super successful later on."

Chloe Song, an economics freshman at LSA, agreed that the initial transition can be daunting. 

"I think that's a good call because it's really stressful," Song said.

The LSA is the largest of the university’s 19 schools and colleges, serving approximately 19,700 undergraduate students. University leaders hope the grade-covering policy gives students the freedom to explore challenging electives without fear of damaging their long-term GPAs. Similar pass/fail or hidden-grade policies for first-year students have existed for decades at institutions such as MIT, Caltech, Wellesley, and Swarthmore.

However, not all U-Mich students are on board. Some argue that shielding grading consequences promotes poor study habits and ignores the root causes of student anxiety.

"I think it's kind of silly," said Talan, a freshman neuroscience major. "I know they say it's to curb mental health and stop people from having mental health crises, but I feel like that is our generation having access to media across the world. That's why their mental health is a little worse, not because they’re worried about grades."

"We’re at the University of Michigan — people tried pretty hard to get here," Talan added. "I feel like grades are taken pretty seriously. And if you're going to try, working as hard as someone who gets a C and passes with the same grade as you is kind of demeaning in a way."

Simran, a sophomore business major, suggested that hiding grades avoids teaching resilience.

"I think having more supportive resources is a better solution than hiding grades," Simran said. "I think there's a lot of challenges that you face in college, and challenging coursework is one of them. It's something you just learn to move through. I've definitely done poorly in classes before, but it's an upward battle at times... it's a very important skill to have."

Others expressed concern that the policy will merely delay academic stress until the second semester.

Andrew Spencer, a biology, health, and society major, said that while he might have personally benefited from the break, he believes the policy will ultimately backfire.

"Overall, it's just going to hurt more," Spencer said. "People are just going to slack off and not care about their grades in the first semester, and then not have the skills themselves for the second semester to come in and have a great work ethic."

Monica Diaz, a junior studying psychology and economics, offered a middle ground, noting that while she understands critics' concerns, the single-semester policy isn't permanent coddling.

"I don't entirely agree with that because I think it's just slowly transitioning them into what it's like to be at a school like the University of Michigan," Diaz said. "Obviously, after the first semester they're not going to be coddled anymore, so I don't really think that's entirely true — but I can definitely see the argument."

item.title: Texas opens season against Texas State as Arch Manning faces a make-or-break college football year
item.description: Arch Manning enters a make-or-break season as Texas hosts Texas State in a lopsided Week 1 college football matchup with the under 59.5 play.
item.content:encoded:
We officially have the first full weekend of college football. From now until the end of the year, we get to watch football essentially all day Saturday and Sunday.

Sure, there will be some breaks in there, and some days that won’t have quite as much on the gridiron. Still, I’m pumped to have it back and have more options for sports betting. I mentioned this in another article, but this is not a great week of games, as most are lopsided games.

We will likely have one here between Texas State and Texas, but there is still reason for intrigue.

STEVE SARKISIAN GIVES EMBARRASSING EXPLANATION FOR TEXAS' COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF LOSS: 'WE WERE TIRED'

Money is a major factor in college sports, but with college football being the king of them, there is money galore. I have to imagine that one of the reasons that Texas State agreed to this game is that the school was paid a lot of money to come play Texas.

Texas State went 7-6 last year, so it wasn’t like they were awful. However, the best team they played last year was probably Arizona State. They played Rice in a bowl game, so perhaps that was their toughest game.

Brad Jackson is back under center for Texas State, so you have to imagine the team will at least know the offense well enough to run coherent plays. Last season he was pretty good. He completed 71% of passes, had 21 touchdowns, and seven interceptions, while racking up 3,224 yards. Greg Burrell, who was their secondary running back last year, steps in as the primary back this year. He averaged 6.7 yards per carry last year, but had just 3 touchdowns.

ARCH MANNING ISN’T BACKING DOWN FROM EXPECTATIONS, AND NEITHER IS STEVE SARKISIAN, AS CFP SEMIS AREN'T ENOUGH

In my opinion, this is a make-or-break season for Texas. I’m not saying their coach will be fired, or anything like that. However, I also wouldn’t rule that possibility out.

The bigger thing to me is that they need to figure out what is going on with their quarterback, Arch Manning.

Coming out of high school, he was one of the highest-regarded prospects potentially ever. In his first season as the primary QB, he was fairly average. He completed just 61.4% of passes, but had 26 touchdowns and seven interceptions to go along with 3,163 yards.

It was a tale of two locations for Manning. At home, he was very good, completing 65% of passes and 19 of his 26 touchdown passes. He only had two of his seven interceptions at home as well. They missed the playoffs despite coming into the season as the top-ranked team in football. Manning is projected to be the No. 1 overall pick in the NFL Draft. I just don’t see it happening if he doesn’t take a major step forward.

This is a much easier way to start the year than what Texas had last year, starting on the road against Ohio State (they face them again, but at home next week). This year, Texas should destroy their opponent to start the season. However, Texas only had two wins last year by more than 21 points. They played a tough schedule, but they also played a lot of close games. There is no lack of talent here, but I don’t see this team scoring a ton of points either. I think Manning will play maybe half the game unless he looks awful, and if he looks awful, they won’t have many points. Give me the under 59.5.

item.title: Abdul El-Sayed hits back at Israel questions, suggests his name and faith are behind press scrutiny
item.description: Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed suggested reporters press him on the Israel-Hamas war because of his name and faith.
item.content:encoded:
Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed suggested that reporters press him about the Israel-Hamas war because of his name and his faith. 

Speaking on Detroit Public Radio’s "MichMash" podcast, El-Sayed pushed back on host Zach Gorchow’s line of questioning about the Israel-Hamas conflict, suggesting that his name and Muslim faith play a role in the media attention surrounding the issue.

"You've been asked many times whether you support a two-state solution regarding the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and you generally say you support equal rights to self-determination for Jewish Israelis and Palestinians," Gorchow said. "Can you tell us, what does that mean?"

MICHIGAN DEM HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED JABS CNN GIVING HIM 'NON-CONSENSUAL COLONOSCOPY' IN RECENT INTERVIEWS

"Zach, with all due respect, this has been hashed and rehashed," El-Sayed began. "This is the MichMash podcast. I'm focused on what's happening for the 10 million people in this state."

El-Sayed then suggested the media’s interest in his stance on the conflict was related to his identity.

MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE CONFRONTED REPEATEDLY OVER ISRAEL’S RIGHT TO EXIST, DEFUNDING THE POLICE

"It's so frustrating to me that people want to make this race about something that's happening 6,000 miles away, when we've got kids who can't afford a next meal here at home," he continued.

The controversial candidate went on to blast the constant line of questioning from members of the press regarding his stance on providing aid to Israel — a topic he has remained staunchly against throughout his campaign.

MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL CALLS AIPAC DONATIONS 'LEGALIZED BRIBERY,' REMAINS SILENT ON OTHER DONATIONS

"I just find it so interesting that I never get asked about this question on the stump," El-Sayed told the host. "But it seems to me that every time I sit down with anybody in the press, it seems that that's the most important question."

El-Sayed continued by suggesting the media’s focus on his stance on Israel could be related to his name and Muslim faith.

EL-SAYED’S HASAN PIKER PROBLEM FOLLOWS HIM TO DEM CONVENTION AS JEWISH VOTERS BREAK RANKS

"It tends to be the first question everybody likes to ask me," he said. "I wonder why? I mean, does it have something to do with my name? Maybe, you know, how I pray?"

He concluded by doubling-down on his assertion that his campaign is focused on the people of Michigan — not the people of Israel.

MICHIGAN DEMOCRATIC SENATE CANDIDATE CLAIMS ISRAEL 'JUST AS EVIL' AS HAMAS

"It's fascinating to me that I'm running to represent ten million people who live here, and you want to ask about people living somewhere else," El-Sayed continued. "And I just think I want to be talking about [the] people living here."

According to data compiled by the Jewish Virtual Library, Michigan is home to 129,225 Jewish residents — which comprise roughly 1.3% of the state’s population.

JEWISH DEMOCRATS ABANDON EL-SAYED FOR GOP RIVAL IN ALL-IMPORTANT BATTLEGROUND STATE

El-Sayed’s comments were of interest to CEO of Axia Public Relations Jason Mudd, who told Fox News Digital his ability to flip the narrative on the press shows a level of message discipline.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"He stayed on message, pivoting to affordability both times he was asked. That's real discipline. But when you listen to the full episode, he never uses the word racist. He questions why the topic keeps coming up and ties it to his name and his faith. He's pointing to bias."

"If El-Sayed were my client, I'd advise him to name the bias claim directly instead of leaving it implied, then answer the follow-up on what his position actually means in the same breath. Right now the framing comes first, and he still hasn't answered the follow-up."

Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed's campaign for comment.

item.title: 9 warning signs of identity theft you should never ignore
item.description: Nine identity theft warning signs range from unfamiliar credit inquiries to SIM swap attacks that can quietly drain your bank account funds.
item.content:encoded:
Identity theft can start quietly. You may not see a drained bank account or a maxed-out credit card. The first warning could be a strange letter in the mail, an unfamiliar inquiry on your credit report or a password-reset alert you never requested.

Those little clues are easy to brush off, but catching them early can give you more time to protect your money, credit and accounts. One unusual message does not automatically mean someone has stolen your identity, so do not panic. Instead, verify what happened and pay attention to anything else that looks out of place.

Here are nine identity theft warning signs you should never ignore.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com

CYBERCRIME LOSSES NEAR $21B: 5 WAYS TO PROTECT YOUR MONEY

A company may contact you after discovering that customer information was exposed. The notice could come from a bank, retailer, employer, healthcare provider, insurer, school or another organization.

Read it carefully. Find out what information may have been involved, when the incident occurred and whether the company is offering steps such as password changes or credit monitoring. Save the notice with your other records.

A breach notice shows possible exposure, not confirmed identity theft. Still, it is a good reason to review your accounts and strengthen your security.

Check your credit reports for hard inquiries you do not recognize. A hard inquiry generally appears when a lender reviews your credit after you apply for credit.

Also look for new accounts, unfamiliar addresses, collections accounts or loans you never requested. Identity thieves may use stolen information to apply for credit before you notice anything unusual.

Check all three major credit bureaus rather than relying on a single report. Details can differ from one report to another, so reviewing only one may leave gaps.

If you find an inquiry or account that does not belong to you, contact the lender using a trusted phone number or website, rather than contact information from a suspicious message.

A bill for a credit card, utility service, medical account or buy-now-pay-later purchase you did not make is a serious warning sign. So is a call from a debt collector about a debt that does not belong to you.

Do not ignore the notice simply because you believe it is a mistake. Ask the organization for details, dispute the account and keep copies of your correspondence.

Be cautious about sharing personal information with an unexpected caller. If you need to contact a company, find its official number independently.

Review checking, savings, credit card, payment app, investment and retirement accounts regularly. Look for small test charges, unfamiliar withdrawals, new payees, password changes, profile updates or transfers you did not authorize.

Scammers sometimes begin with a small transaction to see whether an account is active. Other times, they try to take over the account entirely.

Contact the financial institution immediately through its official app, website or statement. Ask what steps are needed to secure the account, replace cards, investigate transactions and protect any linked accounts.

Turn on account alerts for purchases, transfers, password changes and other important activity. Alerts are useful, but they work best when you still review statements yourself.

Pay attention to unexpected letters or online notices from the IRS, Social Security Administration or a state agency. Examples include a tax return you did not file, benefits you did not request or a claim connected to an employer you do not recognize.

Do not respond using a link or phone number in an unsolicited message. Visit the agency's official website or use a phone number from a statement or a previously verified account.

Keep every notice. Government-related identity theft can take time to resolve, and a clear record of dates and communications may help.

A phone that unexpectedly loses service can have an innocent explanation, such as an outage or billing problem. But it can also be a sign that someone transferred your number to another device or took over your mobile account.

That is exactly what happened to Patricia Escriva, whose phone suddenly lost service before scammers used a SIM swap attack to get into her accounts and steal thousands of dollars. We broke down her story and what you can learn from it in The CyberGuy Report podcast: How hackers drain your bank account in minutes.

If your phone suddenly goes offline and you cannot explain why, treat it as a warning sign. Contact your wireless provider right away from another phone and ask whether there was a recent SIM change, number transfer or account update. A SIM is the small card or digital profile that connects your phone to a mobile network.

Once your number is secure, review important accounts for password resets or login attempts. Ask your carrier about an account PIN or other protections against unauthorized changes.

HEALTHCARE DATA BREACH EXPOSES 3.75M PATIENT RECORDS

An unexpected password-reset email, multifactor authentication code or sign-in alert may mean that someone is trying to access an account. It may also be a fake message designed to trick you into clicking a link.

Do not share a verification code with anyone who calls or messages you. Open the account through its official app or type the website address yourself, then review recent activity and change the password if needed.

Start with your primary email account. Email often acts as the doorway to password resets for banking, shopping, healthcare and other services. Use a long, unique password and turn on multifactor authentication, which requires an extra verification step beyond your password.

Avoid reusing passwords. If one website is breached, a reused password may give criminals an opportunity to try the same combination elsewhere.

A sudden wave of calls, texts or emails that use your correct name, address, family details or account information deserves attention. This does not prove identity theft, but it may indicate that personal data is circulating among scammers.

Be especially cautious when a message creates urgency, demands payment, asks for a verification code or tells you to move money to "protect" it. Banks, government agencies and legitimate companies do not need you to hand over a one-time code to keep your account safe.

Instead of replying, contact the organization through a trusted channel. Then review your accounts, credit reports and recent security alerts.

An unfamiliar mailing address on a credit report, a changed email address on an account or a notification that your identity was verified somewhere you do not recognize can signal an attempted takeover.

Review account recovery information, authorized users, linked devices and connected apps. Remove anything you do not recognize and change the password from a trusted device.

If the change involves a bank, credit card, phone provider or government account, contact that organization promptly. A small profile change can be an early step in a larger attempt to control the account.

First, slow down and verify the information. A suspicious text may be a scam, and a legitimate account alert may be the result of a family member's purchase or a forgotten subscription.

If the activity is confirmed or you cannot explain it, take these important steps:

Use a trusted number or official app. Ask the organization to secure the account and investigate.

A credit freeze restricts access to your credit file, making it harder for someone to open new credit in your name. Place a freeze with all three major credit bureaus if appropriate for your situation.

A fraud alert asks lenders to take extra steps to verify your identity. It provides another layer of protection and works differently from a credit freeze.

Change important passwords, use a password manager to create and store strong, unique passwords, review recovery settings and add account protections through your wireless provider.

Check banking, credit cards, payment apps, investments, retirement, healthcare, utilities and government services.

Save breach notices, screenshots, dates, names, dispute numbers and copies of letters.

If you confirm that someone has used your identity, report it to the Federal Trade Commission at IdentityTheft.gov. The site will help you create an FTC Identity Theft Report and build a personalized recovery plan. You can also use that report when working with credit bureaus, businesses and debt collectors to dispute fraudulent accounts or information. Some companies may also ask for a police report.

If your information appears in a breach, you may not be able to remove it completely. Focus on making the exposed information less useful: freeze your credit, secure your accounts, limit unnecessary public information and keep watching for new warning signs.

You can take many important steps to protect yourself, including checking your accounts, using unique passwords and freezing your credit. An identity theft monitoring service can add another layer by watching for signs that your personal or financial information may be misused.

Depending on the service and plan you choose, monitoring can include credit reports, checking and savings accounts, investments and 401(k) accounts, bank account takeovers, home title changes, phone takeovers, identity verification, dark web exposure, data breaches and social media activity.

That broader monitoring can be helpful because identity theft can show up in more places than your credit report. If fraud occurs, restoration support may also help reduce the burden of dealing with calls, paperwork and disputes.

Monitoring works best as an added layer of protection rather than a replacement for good security habits. Continue reviewing your accounts, watching for unusual activity and acting quickly when something looks wrong . See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com

NEW BANK SCAM LAWS COULD STOP SUSPICIOUS PAYMENTS

Identity theft often gives you warning signs before serious damage is done. A strange charge, an account you do not recognize or even a password-reset alert you never requested can be your cue to take a closer look. Trust your gut when something feels off, verify what happened and act quickly to lock down your accounts and credit. A few minutes spent checking now could save you a much bigger headache later. The key is to stay alert without living in fear. Keep an eye on your accounts, use strong security protections and know what steps to take if your information ends up in the wrong hands.

item.title: Deprogrammed: Ex-OnlyFans manager finds Jesus and goes on a mission to save young women
item.description: Former OnlyFans manager Victoria Sinis says sexual liberation is "actually the thing that's crushing us" and shares how Christian faith set her free.
item.content:encoded:
Once trapped under the temptation of wealth from the digital exploitation of young women’s bodies, Victoria Sinis is now free from a sordid life as an OnlyFans manager after reclaiming her faith in Jesus.

"Coming from someone that believed the lie that sexual liberation and sexual empowerment was to sleep with people, to show off your body as much as possible, to make money off doing that, and now coming into Christian faith… I see things with a totally new set of values," Sinis told Fox News Digital.

"We paint [sexual liberation] as freedom, but it’s actually the thing that’s crushing us… [It is] actually the thing that's destroying you. It's the thing that's crushing you. It's a thing that makes you more insecure. It’s the thing that makes you feel worse," she continued.

PLAYBOY'S CELEBRITY-DRIVEN RELAUNCH FACES CREDIBILITY TEST IN ONLYFANS ERA, EXPERT SAYS

Sinis, whose work as a manager for an OnlyFans agency in Australia began during the pandemic in an effort to improve her finances while reducing the amount of hours she was working in hospitality, now highlights her experience online, exposing the dark underbelly of the adult industry while saving girls from falling prey to the platform.

"Once you open up the door for sexuality to be able to have any desire that you want fulfilled, people have to understand it's a never-ending pit. It just keeps going. And so the reason why faith has such strong values around sexuality is because it understands the dangers of when you open that door — it's very hard to close it," Sinis said.

"When you understand in a faith lens of, ‘Wow, there's a reason for this, and it's made in a specific and particular way to be able to best express this thing,’ it's the most freedom you can ever have," she said.

"I saw firsthand how things like OnlyFans are really destroying men…. There is an entire multi-billion dollar industry that is targeting men, to be able to harness their weakest essence to get them addicted to these platforms, to make money off of them. And in return, it is heightening their loneliness, their depressions, their anxiety, their disconnectedness, their struggles with being able to build healthy relationships," she continued.

'HARRY POTTER' ACTOR SAYS ONLYFANS VIDEOS EARNED HER MORE THAN HER ENTIRE ACTING CAREER

"These platforms are really destructive for men, and we need to understand that the more we encourage this, the more that we're actually hurting men as much as we are hurting women," she relayed.

Sinus was catapulted over time into searching for a good deed to redeem herself and outdo the bad she felt she was doing. That journey led her back to the church she visited as a child, where she encountered a sermon that "instantaneously clicked" with her spirit, reconnected her with Jesus and helped her leave the industry for good.

Sinis, who now travels the world speaking about her experience in the adult industry, points to social media as a main culprit in glamorizing lifestyles that make children and young people idolize career choices like OnlyFans.

"Parents are so unaware of what is truly influencing their child. If they have a phone, if they have a laptop, if their friend has a phone, if their friend has an iPad, and they have unlimited Internet access to any type of social media platform, they're going to be influenced by those things unless values are instilled within them that help them to understand that what they're seeing online is not real," she revealed.

FORMER DISNEY STAR DAVID HENRIE REJECTED 'SECULAR' HOLLYWOOD LIFESTYLE AFTER LIFE-CHANGING MONASTERY VISIT

"I had two 15-year-olds at a private Catholic school in a fantastic area in Melbourne, Australia, tell me that they loved watching this OnlyFans influencer, because she seemed happy and can travel. And so sometimes it's the most innocent of things, but they're now equating to OnlyFans with being happy and travel[ing] — so now they believe that the only way to be happy and to travel is through OnlyFans," Sinis added.

"This is the sex industry. It is the same consequences, the same mental health ramifications and the same struggles as any other woman in the sex history. And we need to treat it that way and understand that the struggles that the girls have in OnlyFans really is the same as anyone in escorting prostitution, brothels.. and that way we're able to act in accordance with that and be able to truly help these women to leave [the industry]," Sinis said.

An OnlyFans spokesperson told Fox News Digital, "OnlyFans was designed to empower creators to control and monetize their content, and individual creators determine what content they choose to create and how they engage with their audience. Since the platform was established in 2016, more than $30 billion has been paid out to creators around the world, including more than $6 billion in 2025."

item.title: Trump pardons Jay-Z associate Emory Jones after federal drug conviction
item.description: Alice Marie Johnson revealed Trump granted clemency to 30 individuals, including Emory Jones, a Roc Nation executive and Jay-Z's longtime associate.
item.content:encoded:
Emory Jones, longtime friend and business associate of Jay-Z, has been granted a pardon by President Donald Trump.

Jones, who is now an executive in Jay-Z's Roc Nation, was sentenced to nearly 16 years in 2000 on federal drug charges. Thanks in part to a letter from the hip-hop mogul, his sentence was reduced by 37 months, but now, Trump has given him a completely clean slate.

The news was shared this week by Alice Marie Johnson, who was pardoned by Trump in 2020 after being sentenced to life in prison on a nonviolent drug charge in 1996. She now works with the White House as the "pardon czar."

JELLY ROLL GRANTED PARDON BY TENNESSEE GOVERNOR IN CHRISTMAS SEASON CLEMENCY DECISION

"Yesterday was a powerful day for second chances," Johnson wrote on Instagram. "I am deeply grateful to President @realdonaldtrump for granting clemency and pardons to 30 deserving individuals whose cases we carefully reviewed and brought forward—and to the White House Counsel team, led by Will Scharf, for the hard work behind these decisions."

She added, "Among them is Emory Jones, who served nearly 16 years in federal prison and came home determined to build a different life. Today he is an entrepreneur and creative leader whose journey reminds us how much people can grow—and how much good they can still do."

TODD CHRISLEY RECALLS EMOTIONAL PHONE CALL WITH DAUGHTER SAVANNAH AFTER CONTROVERSIAL TRUMP PARDON

In 1999, Jones pleaded guilty to a charge of conspiracy to distribute cocaine. The following year, he was sentenced to 188 months, nearly 16 years, in prison, with five years supervised release.

Jones' legal team submitted a request for a reduction of his sentence in 2009, and as part of their request, they submitted a series of letters from people familiar with Jones, including Jay-Z.

In a letter to the judge, Jay-Z, whose real name is Shawn Carter, wrote that he'd be offering Jones an executive assistant job with Roc Apparel Group upon his release, with a starting salary of $50,000.

I believe his attributes, including intelligence, interpersonal skills and solid work ethic will be a significant asset for my organization."

In another letter, Jones himself wrote about his conviction, saying, "Of all the excuses that I could have attributed my demise to, I chose not to use a single one. Excuses are tools of the incompetent and only build monuments to nothingness."

Nothing monetary because you can't put a price on love and support. However, you do owe them the privilege and opportunity to see you do something extremely positive with your life."

item.title: Legendary agent explains how Deshaun Watson's $230 million contract has crippled the Browns
item.description: Deshaun Watson's $230 million fully guaranteed contract has crippled the Cleveland Browns' salary cap, with an $86.2 million dead cap hit looming in 2027.
item.content:encoded:
The Cleveland Browns hoped when they acquired Deshaun Watson in 2022 that he would have a major impact on the franchise, and revisiting the trade four years later, they weren’t wrong.

What kind of impact, exactly, has Watson had on the Browns? A disastrous one. The team gave up five draft picks, including three first-rounders, and then signed Watson to a five-year, $230 million fully guaranteed contract, the largest amount of guaranteed money given to a player in NFL history.

Watson was suspended for 11 games in 2022 after facing several sexual assault allegations from his time with the Houston Texans. Watson has played only 19 games in four seasons with the Browns and has disappointed on the field. Legendary sports agent Leigh Steinberg explained that while Watson has hurt the Browns on the field with his play, his exorbitant contract has crippled the team's salary-cap flexibility.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"The fact that they've got that contract on Cleveland's roster, which is all guaranteed, makes it very difficult to do what is advanced caponomics, which is to take a high salary, all of which counts against the cap, and supplement it with a new signing bonus and extend the contract out over a series of years," Steinberg told OutKick in a recent interview.

"That's the modus operandi to fit talented players into a cap. But when all the money is guaranteed, there's no way to escape the cap hit."

The Watson contract is so onerous that the Browns were forced to push his cap hit into the future beyond the term of his five-year contract by using void years. Early in Watson’s contract, they lessened his cap hit in order to build around him and pushed a ton of money into the future.

Now they are feeling the constraints of Watson’s deal.

Here are Watson’s cap hits from 2022 through 2030: In 2022, it was $9.4 million, followed by $19 million, nearly $28 million, nearly $36 million and a $40.2 million cap hit this season.

LEGENDARY SPORTS AGENT TALKS ABOUT THE RAMS USE OF 'CAPONOMICS' TO BRING AARON DONALD OUT OF RETIREMENT

Next season, despite not being on the Browns' roster after his contract expires this season, Watson will have an astronomical $86.2 million cap hit, followed by a $25.7 million cap hit in 2028, nearly $17 million in 2029 and $8.9 million in 2030. In all likelihood, the Browns will have to further leverage their future cap space because carrying an $86.2 million cap charge for a player who will likely not be on their roster next year would be crippling to a front office trying to build a competitive roster.

If the Browns decide to leave that $86.2 million entirely on next season’s cap, it would account for more than a quarter of their salary cap. Despite the cap continuing to rise year after year, a cap hit that high is not tenable for a team trying to win games and spend big in free agency.

The Browns, despite having a 9-10 record in Watson’s starts, named him their Week 1 starting quarterback. Watson has completed 61.2% of his passes for 3,365 yards with 19 touchdowns and 12 interceptions in his tumultuous tenure.

Watson has not played since he tore his right Achilles tendon in October 2024, and re-tore it during rehab in January 2025.

The Browns hope Watson can recapture some of the magic he had with the Houston Texans this season under new head coach Todd Monken because, if he can, his massive cap hit won't hurt as much.

But Steinberg isn’t sure Watson will play well enough to fend off backup Shedeur Sanders, and start the whole season.

"Now, if Deshaun Watson were to come back to what he was at Clemson or with Houston, he started out like he was going to have a spectacular career and then because of offseason issues and injuries, the wheels came off. And so, while he's been designated the starter now, it's unclear whether or not he'll hold that till the end of the year," Steinberg said.

Watson is only 30 years old, and Steinberg mentioned quarterbacks who have been effective despite being much older than Watson.

"He's not too old. As we've seen with Aaron Rodgers and Tom Brady, players can play deep into their 40s and still be effective at that position, but he's got to be a little rusty," Steinberg said.

item.title: 'Pod Save America' hosts mock JD Vance over ‘blood libel’ definition before botching it themselves
item.description: Jon Favreau and Jon Lovett mocked JD Vance's use of "blood libel" but stumbled through wrong definitions of the antisemitic accusation.
item.content:encoded:
"Pod Save America" co-hosts Jon Favreau and Jon Lovett mocked Vice President JD Vance during a Wednesday episode for his use of the term "blood libel," only to offer incorrect explanations of the centuries-old antisemitic accusation. They eventually arrived on its historical definition, but drew criticism from Commentary senior editor Seth Mandel.

The hosts laughed while discussing Vance’s usage and suggested he was interpreting the phrase literally through "bloodline" and being "liable," before Lovett offered his own definition.

"The blood libel is that we killed Jesus. That’s it. We killed Jesus," he said.

ISRAEL FOREIGN MINISTRY CONDEMNS NEW YORK TIMES PIECE AS 'ONE OF THE WORST BLOOD LIBELS' IN MODERN PRESS

Favreau immediately rejected that explanation but then connected the term to the biblical Passover story in which Israelites marked their doors with lamb’s blood so the plague killing Egypt’s firstborn would pass over their homes.

"No, the blood libel is that Jews supposedly, um, uh, put blood on... this is an Old Testament story... on a house so that when like the angel of death came by, they would skip over the houses with the blood on it but kill the firstborn," he said.

After recognizing that the story was Passover, the hosts eventually read the historical definition of blood libel aloud.

VICE PRESIDENT JD VANCE BLASTS MAMDANI, EL-SAYED, AOC AND OSSOFF IN RAPID-FIRE TIKTOK ROAST

Vance explained his understanding of the term while discussing antisemitism before the Republican Jewish Coalition.

"The idea that because of your genetics, because of your blood, because of your ancestry, you are guilty of a crime that you never committed," Vance said. Jewish Insider reported that Vance used "blood libel" and "blood guilt" interchangeably during the appearance.

Mandel said the hosts’ confusion over the meaning of blood libel reflected a broader problem in how accusations of antisemitism are sometimes dismissed, warning that treating Jewish concerns as exaggerated or unserious can both minimize the history behind such tropes and make it easier for antisemitic rhetoric to persist.

"Anti-Semites know how to graft Medieval blood libels onto baseless accusations against Israel and the Jewish community today. The Jewish victims of these blood libels also, of course, know their history quite well. The Pod Save America hosts represent a third group: the self-righteous ignoramuses who automatically dismiss accusations of anti-Semitism against their political allies," Mandel said in a statement to Fox News Digital on Friday.

CHRISTIAN LEADERS HOLD EMERGENCY SUMMIT IN JERUSALEM TO CONFRONT GLOBAL RISE IN ANTISEMITISM

"If you start from a position of, essentially, ‘the Jews are silly and oversensitive,’ you will set yourself up to look like a fool, as the Pod bros did. You will also only encourage anti-Semitism to continue, as the Pod bros do," he continued.

The U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum defines blood libel as the false allegation that Jews used the blood of non-Jews, typically Christian children, for religious rituals. The museum separately identifies the accusation that Jews were collectively responsible for killing Jesus as another historical form of antisemitism.

The Anti-Defamation League (ADL) similarly describes blood libel as the centuries-old falsehood that Jews murdered Christians, particularly children, to use their blood for religious purposes, including the purported baking of Passover matzah. Such accusations historically helped fuel mob violence and pogroms against Jewish communities.

The ADL reported 9,354 incidents of antisemitic assault, harassment and vandalism in the United States in 2024, the highest annual total since the organization began tracking incidents in 1979. The group said 58% of the incidents included elements related to Israel or Zionism, marking the first time such incidents accounted for a majority of its annual tally.

Fox News Digital reached out to Vance for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

item.title: Miss America contestant reveals surprising day job as Massachusetts police officer
item.description: Ashlyn Mercier became the first police officer named Miss Massachusetts and now competes for the Miss America crown while serving her community.
item.content:encoded:
Ashlyn Mercier has spent her career wearing a badge. Now, she's hoping to wear one of the country's most coveted tiaras.

The Westborough, Massachusetts, police officer is competing in Miss America. The final competition takes place Sept. 6 at the Palm Beach County Convention Center in West Palm Beach, Florida. Mercier is also the first police officer to be named Miss Massachusetts.

"I think there's not one single look for what a female police officer is supposed to look like," Mercier told Fox News Digital. "And if we say that there is, that's just wrong because, at the end of the day, yes, female law enforcement officers only make up approximately 14% of the force in the United States, but we don't have to look a certain way."

NAVY VETERAN TRADES MILITARY UNIFORM FOR MISS GEORGIA SASH FOLLOWING HEARTBREAKING LOSS

"People are so multifaceted, women are so multifaceted, and I'm just trying to show young girls that they can chase all of their dreams simultaneously," Mercier said. "They don't have to pick one thing and make that their entire identity."

The glitzy competition dates to a 1921 beauty contest in Atlantic City, New Jersey, held a year after the 19th Amendment guaranteed women the right to vote. The organization awards scholarships and gives its titleholder a national platform for community service and advocacy.

Mercier hopes to raise awareness of her cause, "Nick's Courage: One Smile Goes a Mile," named after her younger brother, Nicholas, a two-time pediatric cancer survivor. The initiative aims to bring positivity and hope to children battling critical illnesses. 

In 2025, she took a year off from pageant competition to follow in her father's footsteps and attend the police academy.

WATCH: ACTIVE-DUTY POLICE OFFICER COMPETES IN MISS AMERICA 

"I didn't know if I would ever come back and compete," Mercier said. "I was afraid of what other people would think if I chased both of those dreams at the same time. I also had this dream of becoming a police officer. But what I came to realize is that I can't worry about what other people think. I've got to focus on myself. And it ended up working out for me."

Mercier said the Westborough Police Department has been cheering her on as she balances the competition with her work as an officer. Fox News Digital reached out to the department for comment.

"I'm really fortunate that they have been so incredibly supportive," Mercier said. "I work for an amazing department, and my co-workers have supported me 100% from the moment I told them I was competing as Miss Massachusetts to now being at Miss America. They've shown up to my sendoff parties, they've helped me with my fundraising efforts, they've sent me good luck texts."

"It's really just an honor to be surrounded by people who uplift me," she said. "It really continues to help motivate me to move forward."

Mercier said her career in law enforcement doesn't give her an advantage on the Miss America stage. She's one of the delegates representing the 50 states, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico, each hoping to stand out.

Still, other officers have taken notice.

"I've had thousands of female law enforcement officers across the country commenting on my posts saying that they're rooting for me and that they're inspired by me," Mercier said. "There are also young girls saying that they want to get into law enforcement, and they're inspired by my story. And then, I serve my community in Westborough every single day in my capacity as a police officer, but I also get to serve my community in the role as Miss Massachusetts."

"Those two things are what is so important about the Miss America opportunity," Mercier said. "Yes, we get to dress up. Yes, we get to wear pretty gowns and look beautiful. But, women's empowerment and service are the core. And if you look at it like that, you can see and draw a lot of parallels between Miss America and between my role as Officer Mercier."

Police work has also given Mercier skills she can use in the competition. She said she's comfortable communicating with different people and staying calm in nerve-wracking situations. But one challenge remains.
